subject: Cognitive Science
title: Change Blindness
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Change Blindness.

hook.text: A researcher swaps a conversation partner behind a door. Most people don't notice it's a new person.

buildup.text: This is change blindness—when shifts in a scene go undetected because attention was elsewhere.

discovery.text: It reveals that we don't store a rich mental image. We see detail only where attention lands.

twist.text: Even experts fall for it. Pilots in simulators miss runway changes right in front of them.

climax.text: Our feeling of seeing everything is an illusion built by rapid eye movements and memory fills.

punchline.text: You think you see the whole world. You don't.

quiz.question: What does change blindness reveal about perception?
options: We only see detail where attention is directed

details.summary: Change blindness is the failure to notice large changes in a visual scene when they occur during a brief disruption like a blink or a cut in a video. Even dramatic alterations to color, object identity, or people can go undetected, revealing how little of our visual world we actually encode.
details.whyItMatters: Change blindness reveals that our sense of a rich, detailed visual world is largely an illusion. We encode far less than we think, which matters for design, safety, and legal testimony.
takeaways: Large visual changes can go unnoticed during brief disruptions
Our perception of a detailed visual world is partly illusory
Focused attention on the change location is required to detect it

faq.question: What causes change blindness to occur?
faq.answer: Change blindness happens because the visual system does not store a detailed representation of the entire scene. Without focused attention on the specific location of a change, the brain lacks the before-and-after comparison needed to detect the difference.

faq.question: How is change blindness different from inattentional blindness?
faq.answer: Inattentional blindness means failing to see something unexpected in plain view. Change blindness means failing to notice a change between two views. Both reveal attention limits, but change blindness requires a disruption that masks the change signal.
